Assume AC. Let $X\in\mathbb R^d$ and $Y\in\mathbb R^m$, with $d,m\ge1$, be
jointly multivariate normal with mean $(a,b)$ and positive-semidefinite block
covariance
$$\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\C^T&B\end{pmatrix},$$
where $B$ is positive definite. Then
$$S=A-CB^{-1}C^T$$
is positive semidefinite, and for every $y\in\mathbb R^m$ the probability law
$$K(y,\cdot)=N_d\!\left(a+CB^{-1}(y-b),S\right)$$
is defined. The map $K$ is a probability kernel and is a conditional law of
$X$ given $Y$: for all Borel $E\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and
$F\subseteq\mathbb R^m$,
$$\mathbb P(X\in E,Y\in F)=\int_F K(y,E)\,\mathbb P_Y(dy).$$
The covariance $A$ and the conditional covariance $S$ may be singular.
Positive definiteness of $B$ is required; no pseudoinverse formula for
singular $B$ is asserted.

**Given:** AC and a jointly Gaussian pair with the mean and block covariance
in the Statement.

[A1] AC is assumed by the multivariate-normal realization and zero-cross-covariance independence suppliers. [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F1] A multivariate-normal law may have positive-semidefinite covariance and is characterized by having the stated scalar-normal linear projections; its mean and covariance are the stated $m$ and $\Sigma$. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]].

[F2] Jointly Gaussian blocks with zero cross-covariance are independent, including when either covariance block is singular. [[lem-joint-gaussian-blocks-with-zero-cross-covariance-are-independent]].

[F3] A law is the pushforward probability measure of its random element. [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]].

[F4] Integrating a nonnegative product-measurable function against a finite kernel gives a measurable function of the kernel parameter. [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]].

[F5] Independent random elements have their product joint law. [[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]].

[F6] Tonelli evaluates nonnegative integrals on sigma-finite product spaces. [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]].

[F7] Kernel evaluations are measurable and each probability-kernel section is a probability measure. [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Let $(U_1,U_2)$ be a jointly multivariate-normal vector with mean $(m_1,m_2)$ and covariance
$$\begin{pmatrix}S&0\\0&T\end{pmatrix},$$
where $S$ and $T$ are allowed to be singular positive-semidefinite matrices. Then the random vectors $U_1$ and $U_2$ are independent.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ with a state-space model by
probability kernels as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. If $T=0$, put $\Omega_T=E_0$;
otherwise put $\Omega_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times
F_T$. Let $\mathcal Z_T$ be the corresponding finite-product sigma-algebra
and write $(\Omega_T,\mathcal Z_T,P_T)$ for its finite-horizon probability
space. The law $P_T$ is the unique law supplied by
[[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]]. Let $X_t$ and
$Y_t$ be the coordinate random elements taking values in $E_t$ and $F_t$. For
$t\ge1$, write $Y_{1:t}:=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_t)$ and
$\mathsf F_{1:t}:=F_1\times\cdots\times F_t$ with its finite-product
sigma-algebra; let $\mathsf F_{1:0}$ be a singleton and $Y_{1:0}$ its constant
map. The factors are standard Borel, meaning measurably isomorphic to Polish
spaces ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), and their finite products are standard
Borel ([[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]).

The **initial filtering kernel** $\pi_0:\mathsf F_{1:0}\to E_0$ assigns
$\mu_0$ to the unique empty history; it is the conditional law of $X_0$ given
the trivial history. For $1\le t\le T$, a **filtering kernel at time $t$** is
a probability kernel $\pi_t:\mathsf F_{1:t}\to E_t$ such that
$\omega\mapsto\pi_t(Y_{1:t}(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional
distribution of $X_t$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:t})$. For $1\le t\le T$, a
**predictive kernel at time $t$** is a probability kernel
$\pi_{t|t-1}:\mathsf F_{1:t-1}\to E_t$ whose composition with $Y_{1:t-1}$
is a regular conditional distribution of $X_t$ given
$\sigma(Y_{1:t-1})$. A **finite-horizon smoothing kernel** is a probability
kernel $\psi_T:\mathsf F_{1:T}\to E_0\times\cdots\times E_T$ whose
composition with $Y_{1:T}$ is a regular conditional distribution of the full
state path $(X_0,\ldots,X_T)$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:T})$. Here a regular
conditional distribution is an everywhere probability kernel satisfying the
conditional event identities in
[[def-regular-conditional-distribution]], and a conditional law given a
random element is its data-indexed kernel form in
[[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]].

These kernels are versions: their values can be changed on a measurable set
of observation histories of probability zero without changing the conditional
identities. No density is assumed in these definitions. The state-space model
here is one fixed law. A parametric statistical model is instead a map
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$ from a parameter set to probability laws; its
measurability is not asserted without a parameter sigma-algebra
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

suppliers.exact_facts:
**Given:** AC, a finite horizon $T\ge0$, standard-Borel state spaces
$(E_t,\mathcal E_t)$ and observation spaces $(F_t,\mathcal F_t)$, an initial
probability measure and probability kernels as in the Statement.

[A1] AC states that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function.
[[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] A finite-horizon model supplies standard-Borel state and observation
spaces, an initial law, transition kernels, and observation kernels.
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]

[F2] Under AC these data determine a unique probability law on the interleaved
finite path space with the stated iterated-kernel formula.
[[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]]

[F3] Every finite product of standard-Borel spaces, with its finite-product
sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.
[[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]

[F4] Under AC, a random element with standard-Borel target has a regular
conditional distribution given any sub-sigma-algebra.
[[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]]

[F5] Under AC, an RCD given $\sigma(Y)$ factors through a standard-Borel
random element $Y$ as a probability kernel on its observation space.
[[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]]

[F6] A data-indexed conditional law is a probability kernel whose composition
with the conditioning random element is an RCD.
[[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]

[F7] An RCD is an everywhere probability kernel satisfying all conditional
event identities. [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]

[F8] Filtering, predictive, and smoothing kernels have the definitions and
conditioning sigma-algebras stated above.

exact_manifest_row.title: Filtering and finite-horizon smoothing laws exist
exact_manifest_row.statement:
Assume AC and a finite-horizon state-space model by standard-Borel state and
observation spaces, an initial probability measure, and transition and
observation probability kernels, as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. Let $P_T$ be its finite-horizon
path law. The initial filtering kernel is $\pi_0=\mu_0$ on the singleton
empty-history space. For each $1\le t\le T$, data-indexed filtering and
predictive kernels from [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]] exist. A
data-indexed finite-horizon smoothing kernel for the full state path also
exists, including when $T=0$. The claim is existence of conditional versions
only; it asserts no density, filtering recursion, uniqueness on null
observation histories, or numerical approximation.
exact_manifest_row.axiom_use: Assume AC. It is used through the finite-horizon path-law theorem and the RCD existence and factorization theorems. The finite-product standard-Borel closure result itself is choice-free.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$. For
$0\le t\le T$, let
$(E_t,\mathcal E_t)$ be a standard-Borel state space; for $1\le t\le T$, let
$(F_t,\mathcal F_t)$ be a standard-Borel observation space
([[def-standard-borel-space]]), meaning a measurable space bimeasurably
isomorphic to a Polish space. A probability kernel has probability-measure
sections and measurable evaluations as in
[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Specify an initial probability
measure $\mu_0$ on $E_0$ (a measure of total mass one, as in
[[def-probability-measure]]), transition probability kernels $K_t$ from
$E_{t-1}$ to $E_t$, and observation probability kernels $G_t$ from $E_t$ to
$F_t$, for $1\le t\le T$.

The trajectory space, with the finite product sigma-algebra generated by
measurable coordinate rectangles
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]), is
$$\mathcal Z_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times F_T,$$
with $\mathcal Z_0=E_0$. Its finite-horizon law $P_T$ is the unique probability
law whose ordered iterated kernel integral is
$$\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{t=1}^T K_t(x_{t-1},dx_t)G_t(x_t,dy_t).$$
The product notation means successive integration in the displayed order; it
does not assert the existence of densities. Existence and uniqueness under AC
are proved in [[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]].
Every finite product trajectory space is standard Borel by
[[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]].

The initial and transition laws specify the state evolution, while each
$G_t$ specifies the observation law given the current state in this model.
State evolution by itself therefore does not specify a joint state-observation
law. No density or time-homogeneity assumption is imposed, and no strict
stationarity assumption (shift invariance of all finite-dimensional laws) is
required ([[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]]). This is a
single law, not a parameter-indexed family. The model contract records a
proposed law and makes no claim that it adequately describes an application
([[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]]).

Assume AC. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, standard-Borel spaces
$E_0,\ldots,E_T$ and $F_1,\ldots,F_T$, an initial probability measure
$\mu_0$ on $E_0$, and transition and observation probability kernels
$K_t:E_{t-1}\to E_t$ and $G_t:E_t\to F_t$ for $1\le t\le T$, as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. On the interleaved finite
product space
$$\mathcal Z_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times F_T,$$
there is a unique probability measure whose rectangle probabilities are the
ordered iterated kernel integrals
$$\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{t=1}^T K_t(x_{t-1},dx_t)G_t(x_t,dy_t).$$
The product notation means successive integration in the displayed order.
For $T=0$, the assertion is the initial law $\mu_0$ on $E_0$.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.

Assume AC. Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable random element with standard-Borel target, and let $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be any sub-sigma-algebra. There exists a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\mathcal G$. Every section is a probability measure, including at exceptional sample points, and no countable-generation or completeness assumption on $\mathcal G$ is required.

For this necessarily nonempty target, the construction also supplies a bimeasurable bijection $c:E\to B$ onto a Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$, and a countable algebra $\mathcal A$ which generates $\mathcal S$, separates points, and determines finite measures.

Assume AC. Let $X$ and $Y$ take values in nonempty standard-Borel spaces $(E,\mathcal S)$ and $(T,\mathcal T)$ on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$. Let $L$ be a specified regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$, everywhere a probability kernel. There is a probability kernel $K:T\to E$ such that $L(\omega,\cdot)=K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ simultaneously outside a single null set. In fact, with the stated everywhere-kernel convention, the construction below gives this equality for every $\omega$. Consequently K is a conditional law of X given Y.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ and $Y:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\mathcal T)$ be measurable random elements. A **conditional law of X given Y** is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that $\omega\mapsto K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$ in [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. Thus for every $A\in\mathcal S$ and $H\in\sigma(Y)$,
$$\int_H K(Y(\omega),A)\,dP=P(H\cap\{X\in A\}).$$

Composition with Y makes each evaluation $\sigma(Y)$-measurable, and every section remains a probability by [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. The notation $P(X\in A\mid Y=y)=K(y,A)$ refers to a chosen kernel; it is not a ratio involving the possibly zero probability $P(Y=y)$.

Write $P_Y(B)=P(Y^{-1}(B))$ for the law in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. If a specified countable family $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S$ determines probability measures, two conditional laws K,L agree as measures outside a single $\mathcal T$-measurable $P_Y$-null set. Indeed for each $A\in\mathcal C$ the measurable discrepancy $D_A=\{y:K(y,A)\ne L(y,A)\}$ has null inverse image under Y by [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]]. Hence $P_Y(D_A)=0$ by the law definition; the countable union $D$ is null by [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]], and off D the determining property gives equality of measures. This uses a supplied determining family and makes no AC assertion about obtaining one.

Values on a measurable $P_Y$-null subset may be replaced by a specified fixed probability on E without changing these identities. The inverse image of that subset is measurable null, and all event evaluations are bounded, so the modified event integrals agree. Empty-event evaluations remain zero and whole-target evaluations remain one. Existence on standard-Borel spaces is proved separately; the definition alone does not assert a conditional kernel exists.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\Tau)$ be a measurable random element and $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra. A **regular conditional distribution of X given $\mathcal G$** is a probability kernel $K:(\Omega,\mathcal G)\to(T,\Tau)$ satisfying
$$\int_H K(\omega,A)\,P(d\omega)=P(H\cap\{X\in A\})\qquad(H\in\mathcal G,\ A\in\Tau).$$

“Probability kernel” has the pointwise meaning of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]: every $K(\omega,\cdot)$ is a probability measure, and every evaluation is $\mathcal G$-measurable. Its evaluations lie in $[0,1]$ and are integrable. Thus the testing identity says exactly that $K(\cdot,A)$ is a conditional-expectation version of $1_{\{X\in A\}}$ in [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. Conversely, a probability kernel with these version identities satisfies the displayed definition.

The kernel requirement holds at every sample point. Separate eventwise choices of conditional-expectation versions do not imply it and do not by themselves provide one exceptional set valid for all A. When A is empty the testing identity is zero on both sides, and when A=T it is P(H) on both sides. This defines a property of a supplied kernel and makes no existence or AC assertion.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ with a state-space model by
probability kernels as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. If $T=0$, put $\Omega_T=E_0$;
otherwise put $\Omega_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times
F_T$. Let $\mathcal Z_T$ be the corresponding finite-product sigma-algebra
and write $(\Omega_T,\mathcal Z_T,P_T)$ for its finite-horizon probability
space. The law $P_T$ is the unique law supplied by
[[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]]. Let $X_t$ and
$Y_t$ be the coordinate random elements taking values in $E_t$ and $F_t$. For
$t\ge1$, write $Y_{1:t}:=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_t)$ and
$\mathsf F_{1:t}:=F_1\times\cdots\times F_t$ with its finite-product
sigma-algebra; let $\mathsf F_{1:0}$ be a singleton and $Y_{1:0}$ its constant
map. The factors are standard Borel, meaning measurably isomorphic to Polish
spaces ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), and their finite products are standard
Borel ([[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]).

The **initial filtering kernel** $\pi_0:\mathsf F_{1:0}\to E_0$ assigns
$\mu_0$ to the unique empty history; it is the conditional law of $X_0$ given
the trivial history. For $1\le t\le T$, a **filtering kernel at time $t$** is
a probability kernel $\pi_t:\mathsf F_{1:t}\to E_t$ such that
$\omega\mapsto\pi_t(Y_{1:t}(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional
distribution of $X_t$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:t})$. For $1\le t\le T$, a
**predictive kernel at time $t$** is a probability kernel
$\pi_{t|t-1}:\mathsf F_{1:t-1}\to E_t$ whose composition with $Y_{1:t-1}$
is a regular conditional distribution of $X_t$ given
$\sigma(Y_{1:t-1})$. A **finite-horizon smoothing kernel** is a probability
kernel $\psi_T:\mathsf F_{1:T}\to E_0\times\cdots\times E_T$ whose
composition with $Y_{1:T}$ is a regular conditional distribution of the full
state path $(X_0,\ldots,X_T)$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:T})$. Here a regular
conditional distribution is an everywhere probability kernel satisfying the
conditional event identities in
[[def-regular-conditional-distribution]], and a conditional law given a
random element is its data-indexed kernel form in
[[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]].

These kernels are versions: their values can be changed on a measurable set
of observation histories of probability zero without changing the conditional
identities. No density is assumed in these definitions. The state-space model
here is one fixed law. A parametric statistical model is instead a map
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$ from a parameter set to probability laws; its
measurability is not asserted without a parameter sigma-algebra
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, positive state dimensions $d_0,\ldots,d_T$,
and positive observation dimensions $p_1,\ldots,p_T$. The input is a
linear-Gaussian model from
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]], with
matrices $F_k\in\mathbb R^{d_k\times d_{k-1}}$ and
$H_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k\times d_k}$, initial mean $m_0$, and symmetric
positive-semidefinite covariances $P_0,Q_k,R_k$. Its state and observation
equations are
$$X_k=F_kX_{k-1}+q_k,\qquad Y_k=H_kX_k+r_k,$$
where $q_k\sim N(0,Q_k)$ and $r_k\sim N(0,R_k)$ are centered and mutually
independent across all times and of $X_0$.

The admissible data are vectors $y_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$ for which every
innovation covariance encountered below is positive definite. Positive
definite means $u^TS_ku>0$ for every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$. The
algorithm returns predicted and updated means and covariances and the
innovation and gain at each time. Initialize
$$m_{0|0}=m_0,\qquad P_{0|0}=P_0.$$
For $k=1,\ldots,T$, perform:

1. Predict:
$$m_{k|k-1}=F_km_{k-1|k-1},\qquad P_{k|k-1}=F_kP_{k-1|k-1}F_k^T+Q_k.$$
2. Form the innovation and its covariance:
$$v_k=y_k-H_km_{k|k-1},\qquad S_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}H_k^T+R_k.$$
3. Factor $S_k=L_kL_k^T$ with lower-triangular $L_k$ having positive
diagonal, using
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]].
Solve $L_kU_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}$ and $L_k^TK_k^T=U_k$ by triangular solves. This
defines $K_k^T=S_k^{-1}H_kP_{k|k-1}$, hence
$K_k=P_{k|k-1}H_k^TS_k^{-1}$, without explicitly forming $S_k^{-1}$.
4. Update:
$$m_{k|k}=m_{k|k-1}+K_kv_k,\qquad P_{k|k}=P_{k|k-1}-K_kS_kK_k^T.$$

For $T=0$ the loop is empty and the returned pair is $(m_0,P_0)$. No
inverse of $P_0$, $Q_k$, or $R_k$ is used. This item defines the procedure
and makes no complexity, rounding-error, or numerical-stability claim.

Assume AC. Let $U\in\mathbb R^d$, $q\in\mathbb R^n$, and
$r\in\mathbb R^p$ be mutually independent Gaussian vectors with
$$U\sim N_d(m,P),\qquad q\sim N_n(0,Q),\qquad r\sim N_p(0,R),$$
where $P,Q,R$ are symmetric positive semidefinite. Let
$F\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ and $H\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}$, and set
$$X=FU+q,\qquad Y=HX+r,\qquad P^-:=FPF^T+Q,\qquad S:=HP^-H^T+R.$$
If $S$ is positive definite, put $K:=P^-H^TS^{-1}$. Then $(X,Y)$ is jointly
Gaussian with mean $(Fm,HFm)$ and covariance
$$\begin{pmatrix}P^-&P^-H^T\\HP^-&S\end{pmatrix},$$
and for every $y\in\mathbb R^p$ an everywhere-defined conditional law is
$$\mathcal L(X\mid Y=y)=N_n\!\left(Fm+K(y-HFm),\,P^--KSK^T\right).$$
The conditional covariance is positive semidefinite even if $P$, $Q$, or
$R$ is singular. It also equals the Joseph expression
$$ (I-KH)P^-(I-KH)^T+KRK^T.$$
No inverse of a state, process-noise, or measurement-noise covariance is
used.

**Given:** AC, mutually independent Gaussian vectors and the matrices in the
Statement, with $P,Q,R$ positive semidefinite and $S$ positive definite.

[A1] AC is used by the multivariate-normal and conditional-Gaussian suppliers.
[[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F1] A multivariate normal law is defined for every symmetric
positive-semidefinite covariance, including singular ones, and its linear
projections have the corresponding scalar normal laws.
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]].

[F2] A finite stack of mutually independent Gaussian vectors is jointly
Gaussian with block-diagonal covariance; no block must be invertible.
[[lem-finite-independent-gaussian-vectors-form-joint-multivariate-normal]].

[F3] Every finite-dimensional positive-semidefinite operator has a unique
positive-semidefinite square root. [[thm-non-negative-square-root-exists-and-is-unique]].

[F4] For a jointly Gaussian pair with positive-semidefinite block covariance
and positive-definite observed block $B$, the everywhere-defined conditional
law has mean $a+CB^{-1}(y-b)$ and covariance $A-CB^{-1}C^T$, which is
positive semidefinite; the state covariance may be singular.
[[thm-multivariate-normal-conditional-law]].

exact_proof_steps.text: By [F2], the stack $(U,q,r)$ is jointly Gaussian with mean $(m,0,0)$ and covariance $\operatorname{diag}(P,Q,R)$. For any $a\in\mathbb R^n$ and $b\in\mathbb R^p$, the scalar $a^TX+b^TY$ is a linear projection of this stack, so it is normal by [F1]; thus $(X,Y)$ is jointly Gaussian. Since $q$ is independent of $U$ and centered, $\operatorname{Cov}(X)=F\operatorname{Cov}(U)F^T+\operatorname{Cov}(q)=FPF^T+Q=P^-$. Since $Y=HX+r$ and $r$ is independent of $X$ and centered, $\mathbb E X=Fm$, $\mathbb E Y=HFm$, $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=P^-H^T$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(Y)=HP^-H^T+R=S$. Hence the block covariance is the one displayed in the Statement and is positive semidefinite as a covariance matrix. Also $P^-\succeq0$, since $u^TP^-u=(F^Tu)^TP(F^Tu)+u^TQu\ge0$ for every $u$. Assume AC. Fix a finite-horizon model from
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]] with
state and observation equations
$$X_k=F_kX_{k-1}+q_k,\qquad Y_k=H_kX_k+r_k\qquad (1\le k\le T),$$
where $X_0\sim N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$, the centered Gaussian noises $q_k,r_k$ are
mutually independent across times and from $X_0$, and $P_0,Q_k,R_k$ are
symmetric positive semidefinite. Let the parameters and observations be
admissible for [[alg-kalman-filter]], so the recursively formed innovation
covariances
$$S_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}H_k^T+R_k$$
are positive definite for every $1\le k\le T$. Run that algorithm from
$m_{0|0}=m_0$ and $P_{0|0}=P_0$. Then, for each $0\le k\le T$, the map
$$\pi_k(y_{1:k},\cdot)=N_{d_k}(m_{k|k}(y_{1:k}),P_{k|k})$$
is an everywhere-defined filtering kernel for $X_k$ given $Y_{1:k}$ in the
sense of [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. The empty history at $k=0$ is a
singleton, and $\pi_0=N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$. In particular, these recursions
give an exact Gaussian conditional-law version at every observation history;
each $P_{k|k}$ is positive semidefinite. Singular initial, process,
measurement, predicted-state, and filtered-state covariances are allowed.
Equivalently, the covariance update can be written in Joseph form
$$P_{k|k}=(I-K_kH_k)P_{k|k-1}(I-K_kH_k)^T+K_kR_kK_k^T.$$
Only the innovation matrices being solved must be positive definite. No
pointwise uniqueness of a conditional-law version on null histories,
observation-density assumption, or numerical-stability claim is made.
